lead.t: Infection is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma
lead.s: Internal Medicine CAT 1 (MBChB 4), 2022: liver, pancreas and bone marrow, 30 MCQ

b: Epidemiology: commonest primary liver cancer; male to female about 3-8 : 1 ; very common in sub-Saharan Africa and East Asia.

Risk factors: chronic hepatitis B (about 200-fold risk, and HBV can cause HCC even without cirrhosis) , hepatitis C, cirrhosis of any cause , alcohol , aflatoxin B1 (contaminated maize and groundnuts; the p53 codon 249 mutation), NAFLD/NASH
Pathogenesis: repeated injury and regeneration, viral DNA integration and aflatoxin-induced mutations cause dysplastic nodules, then carcinoma. Vascular invasion (portal vein) is common.

Presentation: weight loss, right upper quadrant pain or mass, decompensation of known cirrhosis (new ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy), paraneoplastic features (hypoglycaemia, polycythaemia, hypercalcaemia), rupture with haemoperitoneum.
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) raised; above 1000 ng/mL is highly suggestive (it can be normal in some HCCs and raised in other conditions).
sec.s: Liver tumours: benign, primary malignant and metastatic

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B develops hepatocellular carcinoma. Molecular studies reveal inactivation of p53. Which of the following best describes the normal role of p53 in preventing tumor development?
o: It encourages new blood vessel growth.
It triggers cell death in damaged cells.
qs.e: p53 is a tumor suppressor gene that acts as a 'guardian of the genome'. Its normal functions include inducing cell cycle arrest in response to DNA damage, promoting DNA repair, and initiating apoptosis (programmed cell death) if the damage is irreparable. Inactivation of p53 allows cells with damaged DNA to survive and proliferate, increasing the risk of cancer development.

es.q: Compare Hepatitis B (HBV) and Hepatitis C (HCV) regarding their rates of chronicity in adults and their respective associations with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
es.m: HBV leads to chronicity in 5-10% of infected adults, whereas HCV chronic infection occurs in approximately 85% of cases. Both HBV (via the HBx protein) and HCV are significant risk factors for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with symptoms concerning for acute viral hepatitis. His serological markers indicate HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs negative, and Anti-HBc IgM positive. 1. Interpret these serological findings. What specific phase of HBV infection do they represent?
es.m: 1. These serological findings represent the **'window period'** of acute HBV infection. During this phase, HBsAg has disappeared, and Anti-HBs antibodies have not yet fully developed, leaving Anti-HBc IgM as the sole marker of acute infection. 2. A positive HBeAg indicates **high infectivity and active viral replication**. 3. Both **chronic HBV** and **chronic HCV** infections are significant risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: List the major risk factors associated with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) and identify a key laboratory marker highly suggestive of this malignancy.
es.m: Major risk factors for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) include: 1. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) infection (1 mark) 2. Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) infection (1 mark) 3. Chronic alcohol use (1 mark) 4. ai.summary: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver cancer, often arising in the context of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis. Diagnosis relies on imaging and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels, with staging guiding treatment decisions. Management focuses on curative or palliative options depending on disease extent.

sections.p: Hepatocellular carcinoma is a malignant tumor originating from hepatocytes, the main cells of the liver. It is a major cause of cancer-related death worldwide, particularly in regions with high rates of chronic viral hepatitis.
b: Often develops in patients with underlying chronic liver disease, especially cirrhosis from any cause.
Diagnosis is typically made using imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI) and elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels.

t.b: Detects liver lesions and assesses their characteristics.
A tumor marker that can be elevated in HCC.

sections.p: HCC staging systems, like the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging system, integrate tumor burden, liver function, and patient performance status to guide treatment and predict prognosis.
b: Early-stage HCC is often asymptomatic and amenable to curative treatments.
Advanced-stage HCC is associated with poor prognosis and requires palliative management.

sections.p: Chronic viral hepatitis B and C are the leading causes globally. Other significant risk factors include alcohol-related cirrhosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and certain inherited metabolic disorders.
b: Chronic Hepatitis B infection
Chronic Hepatitis C infection
Alcoholic liver disease (cirrhosis)
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)/Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)
Cirrhosis from any cause (e.g., autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease)
Aflatoxin exposure (from moldy food, common in some tropical regions)

sections.p: Early HCC is often asymptomatic and detected during screening for chronic liver disease. As it progresses, patients may develop symptoms related to liver dysfunction or the tumor itself.
b: Abdominal pain or discomfort, especially in the upper right quadrant.
Unexplained weight loss.
Fatigue and weakness.
Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes).
Abdominal swelling (ascites).
Nausea and vomiting.

sections.p: Diagnostic workup aims to confirm the presence of HCC, assess its extent, and evaluate the underlying liver function.

t.b: Assesses the degree of liver damage and dysfunction.
Checks for anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukocytosis.
Evaluates the liver's synthetic function and clotting ability.
Identifies chronic hepatitis B or C infection as a cause.
Primary screening tool for HCC in at-risk individuals.
Provides detailed imaging of liver lesions and vascularity.

sections.p: Complications arise from tumor progression, liver failure, or treatment side effects. Urgent medical attention is needed for signs of decompensated cirrhosis or tumor rupture.
b: Gastrointestinal bleeding (from varices or tumor erosion).
Hepatic encephalopathy (confusion due to liver failure).
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP).
Ascites refractory to diuretics.
Tumor rupture with hemoperitoneum.
Acute liver failure.

sections.p: Treatment strategies are tailored to the stage of HCC, liver function, and patient's overall health, aiming for cure, local control, or palliation.
b: Curative options (for early-stage HCC): Surgical resection, liver transplantation, or ablation (e.g., radiofrequency ablation).
Loco-regional therapies (for intermediate-stage HCC): Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) or radioembolization (TARE) to control tumor growth.
Systemic therapy (for advanced-stage HCC): Targeted therapies (e.g., sorafenib, lenvatinib) or immunotherapy to slow disease progression.
Supportive care: Management of ascites, encephalopathy, and nutritional support.

sections.p: Regular surveillance is crucial for early detection in at-risk populations. Prevention strategies focus on managing underlying liver disease and avoiding risk factors.
b: Screening with ultrasound and AFP every 6 months for patients with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B.
Hepatitis B vaccination to prevent primary infection.
Antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B and C to reduce liver inflammation and fibrosis.
Limiting alcohol consumption.
Weight management and healthy diet to prevent/manage NAFLD.
Avoiding exposure to aflatoxins.

sections.p: Other liver lesions or conditions can mimic HCC, requiring careful differentiation.
b: Benign liver tumors (e.g., hemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia).
Liver metastases from other primary cancers.
Cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer).
Abscesses or granulomas.

sections.p: Certain findings can be misleading, necessitating a comprehensive clinical assessment.
b: Normal AFP levels can occur in patients with confirmed HCC.
Elevated AFP can be seen in non-cancerous liver conditions (e.g., active hepatitis, cirrhosis).
Imaging findings can be equivocal, especially for small lesions or in the presence of severe fatty liver or cirrhosis.
Patients with chronic liver disease may have baseline abnormalities in LFTs that can mask or be confused with changes due to HCC.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe abdominal pain.
Vomiting blood or passing black, tarry stools.

faq.q: What is the main risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma?
faq.a: Chronic infection with Hepatitis B or C virus, leading to cirrhosis, is the most significant risk factor globally.
Yes, early-stage HCC can be cured with treatments like surgery, liver transplant, or ablation, especially if detected during screening.
Yes, regular screening with ultrasound and AFP for individuals at high risk (e.g., those with cirrhosis) is crucial for early detection and better outcomes.
